History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
- 45-year-old female hotel housekeeper with a 3–4-month history of progressively painful, itchy, cracked palmar skin likely representing irritant contact dermatitis related to cleaning-chemical exposure.

History:
- Presenting complaint: “Soreness” and cracking of the skin on palms and fingers; severe dryness.
- Onset/Duration: Began ~4 months ago soon after starting a new housekeeping position; gradually worsened.
- Progression: Now “hurts a lot,” preventing her from working; off work for the past 3 days.
- Exacerbating factors: Direct contact with cleaning agents; patient seldom wears gloves.
- Relieving/attempted treatments: Over-the-counter E45 emollient and an unspecified antihistamine—no relief.
- Associated symptoms:
  • Intermittent itch.  
  • Occasional bleeding only after scratching.  
  • Mild generalized dryness of legs.  
  • Denies fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel or urinary changes. Appetite normal.
- Review of systems: Negative for systemic, GI, GU, respiratory, or constitutional symptoms.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
  • Medication: Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- No previously diagnosed skin disorders, eczema, or dermatitis reported.

Social History:
- Occupation: Hotel housekeeper; frequent exposure to bathroom cleaning chemicals; often omits glove use.
- Tobacco: Never smoker.
- Alcohol: ~2 pints beer per week.
- Drugs: Denies.
- Recent work impact: Absent from work ×3 days due to hand pain/dysfunction.

Family History:
- Diabetes mellitus in family.
- No known dermatologic, asthma, or bowel disease.

Physical Examination:
- (Tele-visit) No vitals provided.
- Patient-reported findings: Marked palmar dryness, fissuring, cracking; no spontaneous bleeding; intermittent itch.

Investigations:
- None performed or documented.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Palmar dermatitis (probable irritant contact dermatitis)
  • Assessment: Temporal link to new job and unprotected chemical exposure; symptoms of pain > itch; localized to contact areas.
  • Plan:
    – Avoid irritants; wear protective gloves consistently at work.  
    – Prescribe a topical corticosteroid cream (agent/strength not specified).  
    – Prescribe a high-strength emollient; apply liberally 3–4×/day for 10–14 days.  
    – Reassess in 1–2 weeks; return sooner if worsening or spreading.

Issue 2 – Type 2 diabetes mellitus
  • Assessment: No acute concerns raised during visit.
  • Plan:
    – Continue metformin.  
    – Routine diabetes follow-up per primary care (not discussed in detail today).

Issue 3 – Occupational impairment
  • Assessment: Hand pain/fissures causing functional limitation and work absence.
  • Plan:
    – Provide guidance on skin protection to facilitate return to work.  
    – Offer medical certificate if required by employer (not expressly requested).  
    – Reevaluate occupational accommodations at follow-up.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Irritant contact dermatitis – High likelihood: Direct chemical exposure, predominant pain/fissuring, correlation with workplace change.
2. Allergic contact dermatitis – Moderate likelihood: Possible sensitization to cleaning agents; consider if no improvement with avoidance and steroids.
3. Chronic hand (atopic) eczema – Low likelihood: Chronic dry fissured skin but lacks atopic history and has clear occupational trigger.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected: Objective vitals, visual hand exam findings, medication doses, comprehensive allergy review (patient states none), immunization status, labs or HbA1c for diabetes.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; occasional incomplete phrases but clinical content understandable.
